<!-- /at-a-glance -->

valiwatt validates and monitors a forecast of Québec's hourly electricity demand the way a model-risk team would.
The project is about the checks around the forecast: how the model is tested before it is trusted, how it is watched
once it runs, and what it says when it should no longer be trusted.

**What it measures.** The validation report measures the forecast's error on 2020–2023, out of sample, against the
model v1 shipped and against v1's form on the same weather forecast, under a decision rule fixed in the plan before
any v2 replay; how often its prediction intervals cover the actual demand, overall and group by group; what the
monitor recommended when 2023 was rehearsed and 2024 replayed hour by hour, under rules frozen before v2's 2024
replay; and how often the rules raise a false alarm or miss a real change. Every measured number comes from a tracked
run, and every result carries its evaluation label: 2020–2023 served to choose the model, and 2024 had been seen by
the developers through v1 before v2 was chosen, so neither proves v2 better. Only 2025, held out, can.

**What the freeze covers.** v2's monitoring rules keep v1's logic: v1 tuned them on its 2023 rehearsal, and v1's
departure, made after v1's 2024 results had been seen, changed some of them. v2 re-derived the thresholds, the alarm
levels and the drift inputs for its own model and weather input, and added a day-level criterion for a missing
forecast (plan section 9.3). The rehearsal the report shows, like the 2024 replay, ran on the frozen rules: the rules
hash is unchanged since the freeze, and only files outside the rules (the `NOT_RULES` list: the report code, the break
registry, the command line) changed after it. v2's 2024 replays in the replay ledger carry one model hash and one
frozen-artifact hash (`tests/test_tags.py` checks it); nothing recorded at the freeze ties the rehearsal's model to
it. What backs the order of freeze and replay, and how to check it, is below.

**Status: the box at the top of this page states it**, rendered from the same runs as the model card's status in the
validation report, the reference. It reads *candidate* until a 2025 replay starts; then that the 2025 test of record
did not finish, while it has not; then what that test showed, under the decision rule of
[`docs/plan-v2.md`](docs/plan-v2.md), or, if the owner ruled the 2025 start post hoc, that 2025 is not a held-out
test. v1, the first version, stays in the history at the tag `v1`, its report as published included. What is built:

- the data layer and its gates, the weather forecast included;
- a day-ahead forecast: an additive model of the GAM family on NOAA's National Blend of Models temperature forecast,
  one temperature curve per hour, with the day before's and the week before's demand; walk-forward validation beside
  two comparison models (v1 as shipped, and v1's form on the same forecast); prediction intervals of split-conformal
  shape (without that method's finite-sample coverage guarantee: their coverage is measured out of sample);
- frozen models registered in MLflow;
- a monitor that replays a year hour by hour and recommends *investigate the data*, *recalibrate* or *retrain*, its
  rules frozen by the `rules-frozen-v2` tag before v2's 2024 replay (what backs that order, and how to check it: below);
- the rules' false alarms and blind spots, measured after each replay in a diagnostic run of their own;
- a gate in front of the 2025 replay that finds it clean or refuses it; only a dated ruling of the owner, recorded in
  `AGENTS.md`, lifts a refusal.

Every gate and monitor has a break that makes it fire. The monitor's breaks run in a small synthetic world: they show
that a check can fire, not that it would catch the same fault in real demand.

Read the short version first: the findings told in seven plain points (the question, the forecast, the cold, how
sure it is, 2024 replayed but already seen, what the monitor's silence is worth, and what changed since v1 with the
2025 criteria), each linking to the section of the full report that carries the rest:
[French](docs/report/story.fr.md), the reference; [English](docs/report/story.en.md). The full reports, rendered from
the same runs, are the reference behind it; each opens with an « En bref » block ("In brief" in English):

- validation and monitoring, with the model card and a mapping to SR 11-7 and the NIST AI RMF:
  [French](docs/report/validation.fr.md), the reference; [English](docs/report/validation.en.md);
- data quality: [French](docs/report/dq.fr.md); [English](docs/report/dq.en.md).

**The weather forecast.** The forecast is issued at the end of the day before from a temperature forecast already
issued then: NOAA's National Blend of Models NBS guidance for Montréal-Trudeau (CYUL), from the Iowa Environmental
Mesonet's archive, interpolated to the hour and converted to degrees Celsius. The archive records no arrival time, so
a forecast is assumed available two hours after its issue time; the report measures what one later margin (6 hours
instead of 2) would cost; a longer delay is not measured.
The report also gives the bound with the observed weather of the target hour, which stands in for a perfect weather
forecast; that bound is optimistic, and it issues no recommendation.

## Run it

```sh
uv sync
uv run valiwatt all              # fetch the data, run every check, render the report (see below)
uv run pytest -m "not network"   # the offline tests, every injected break included
uv run pytest -m network         # the live tests only (see below)
```

The live tests check the public endpoints, the quoted licence and standard texts, and that the public figure the
report's section 3.1 quotes is still on its page.

A plain `uv run pytest` runs both sets.

`valiwatt all` downloads the public data into `data/`, then runs the 2024 chain as tracked MLflow runs (stored in
`mlruns/`): data quality, walk-forward validation on 2020–2023 with models fitted from 2019, the frozen models, the
2023 rehearsal and the 2024 replay, the conceptual-soundness run (after the replay, deciding nothing), and the breaks.
It renders the reports into `docs/report/` (French, the reference, and English), stamped with the IDs of the runs they
come from and the hash of the code that made them; a test fails when the code no longer matches the stamp. It never
replays 2025. Neither `data/` nor `mlruns/` is in git: anyone can re-run the chain, and the runs, not the rendered
files, are the source of truth. On a later vintage of the sources, the numbers may differ from the committed reports
(see "A later vintage" below).

Steps can also run one at a time: `valiwatt fetch`, `dq`, `validate`, `freeze --year Y`, `replay --year Y`,
`soundness`, `breaks`, `ledger`, `report`. The 2024 and 2025 replays refuse to run until the monitoring rules are
frozen by the `rules-frozen-v2` tag; the 2023 rehearsal does not need it.
`valiwatt safety` scans git's index (every file the next commit would carry) and every object in the history for anything that must not be published.

**2025, once Hydro-Québec publishes it.** No 2025 demand is to be read before then. The gate cannot enforce all of
it; these rest on the developers' conduct (plan section 11.3; report section 9): that nobody looks at 2025 demand on
the portal before the test of record, nor computes on 2025 records outside the replay command; that a ruling entry
comes only from the owner; and that the run store, which lists the starts that did not finish, is kept until the
render. The 2025 test uses the model frozen for 2024. Its training data end on 2023-12-24, as the report's model card
gives it: the walk-forward embargo leaves out the last 7 days before 2024. The model is therefore two years old by the
end of 2025, by design, and a level drift in demand accepted since then shows as bias (plan section 16).
Afterwards: `valiwatt fetch --through 2025` and `valiwatt dq --through 2025`, then `valiwatt replay --year 2025`, which
runs only by that command and only behind its gate. The gate finds the start clean or refuses it with its evidence; no
flag lifts a refusal, only the owner's ruling entry in `AGENTS.md` does, and `valiwatt evidence` produces what he rules
on, deciding nothing. Every start is recorded, and the earliest is the test of record, unless it stopped before it
finished and a ruling of the owner names the start that takes its place. Nothing of the 2025 vintage is rendered before
the first 2025 start.

**A later vintage.** A clone that fetches after Hydro-Québec has published 2025 reads a later vintage of 2019–2024,
whose records Hydro-Québec may have revised: its numbers may differ from the committed reports, and the 2025
data-quality run lists every revised record. Such a clone's store lacks the replays of record: the report shows them
from their entries in the committed replay ledger, labelled as recorded in the ledger and not re-run here, and says
what only the original store holds.

### Checking the freeze from a clone

The order "rules frozen, then v2's 2024 replay" rests on the annotated tag `rules-frozen-v2` (unsigned: its date was
recorded by the author's own tools) and on the start times the replay ledger records. Nothing outside the repository
anchors that order. The tags must be fetched; a clone of the public repository has them. What a clone can then
check, without data or a run store:

```sh
git cat-file -p rules-frozen-v2      # the tag: its commit, its tagger date (as seconds since 1970), its message
TZ=UTC git for-each-ref --format='%(taggerdate:iso-strict-local)' refs/tags/rules-frozen-v2
                                     # the tag's date, in UTC
uv run python -c 'import json; e = json.load(open("docs/replay-ledger.json"))["replays"]; print(min(x["started_utc"] for x in e if x["freeze_tag"] == "rules-frozen-v2"))'
                                     # the earliest start of a v2 replay in the ledger, in UTC: it comes after
                                     # the tag's date
uv run python -c 'from valiwatt.monitor.run import check_freeze; print(check_freeze())'
                                     # the rule files and dependencies equal the tag's; prints the rules hash
git diff --stat rules-frozen-v2..HEAD -- src/valiwatt config
                                     # what changed since: only files outside the rules may appear (NOT_RULES
                                     # in src/valiwatt/monitor/rules.py, whose comment says they render, scan
                                     # or dispatch); the report code among them also computes what the report
                                     # prints (src/valiwatt/report/soundness.py, the conceptual-soundness
                                     # analysis; src/valiwatt/report/validation.py, the report's own measures),
                                     # but none of it is a rule: the recommendations and the 2025 verdict
                                     # come from the rule files
uv run pytest tests/test_tags.py tests/test_replay_ledger.py
                                     # the tags on their pinned commits, every v2 ledger entry tied to the tag's
                                     # commit and to the rules hash at the tag, and v2's 2024 entries to one model
                                     # hash and one frozen-artifact hash
```

The replay ledger, [`docs/replay-ledger.json`](docs/replay-ledger.json), is committed with each report. It holds one
entry per replay of 2024 or 2025 finished since the history was rewritten (the 2023 rehearsal has none): its run ID,
freeze tag and commit, rules and code hashes, start and end times, MAPE, coverage and recommendations, and for v2 its
evaluation label, its model's hash, its verdicts, the hash of the frozen artifacts that judged it and, for 2025, its
standing. v1's entries stay as they were. `valiwatt report`
appends the replays it lacks before it renders (`valiwatt ledger` does only that); an entry is never rewritten, a run
that disagrees with its entry is refused, and the new content must pass the public-safety scan before it is written.
Its hash is in the report's stamp, so a test fails when it changes after the render.

How it is built, and what each choice was made on: [`docs/plan-v2.md`](docs/plan-v2.md), whose section 0 lists what
had been seen first, v1's 2024 replay and its departure, and the spike whose 2020–2023 results chose v2's family and
input (v1's plan: [`docs/plan.md`](docs/plan.md)). The standards the report maps to, quoted and checked against
their PDFs: [`docs/standards.md`](docs/standards.md).

## The rails

The rules every part of the project follows.

- **No lookahead.** Models, intervals and thresholds are fitted on 2019–2023 only, and the code refuses design
  analysis that reads 2024 or 2025, which are replayed as production. v2 was nevertheless chosen after 2024 had been
  seen through v1 (plan section 0), so its 2024 replay is labelled seen by the developers. Validation is walk-forward
  with an embargo. A forecast is used only from the time it is assumed available, and any result that leans on
  observed weather in place of a weather forecast says so. The replay reads raw records, forecasts included, through
  a clock that refuses anything later.
- **A check that cannot fail is not a check.** Every gate and monitor has a test that injects the fault it must catch:
  a duplicated hour, a misplaced record, an impossible value, a sensor outage, a day no forecast fed, a reading past
  the clock, a shifted demand level, intervals made too narrow, a moved freeze tag. `valiwatt breaks` runs them all as
  a tracked run, and the report refuses to render if any break fails. Each break's label says what its test checks.
  Most labels say what the check does with the fault it is given. Some say what the check must not do with an input
  it must leave alone. A control passes only by staying quiet. The monitor's breaks run on synthetic data: they show
  that a check can fire, not that it would catch the same fault in real demand.
- **Numbers come from runs.** The reports, and the box at the top of this page, are rendered from tracked MLflow runs;
  the report's stamp holds the box's hash, so a test fails when it is edited by hand. Every measured value comes from
  a run. The design constants the report templates write in numerals are read from the runs or from the code.
  `tests/test_report_constants.py` checks this. It reads the templates' text, the strings their code prints and the
  numbers their printed expressions write. It allows only a few kinds of numerals there: section, plan and standard
  references, version names, the dates of the owner's rulings, facts of the calendar, the constants of a formula and
  the numbering of a list. Some numbers are not checked. Numbers written out in words are not, such as the six model
  families of the preliminary trial. Neither are the numbers the templates' logic compares against, nor the arguments
  of their filters. Nor are the break labels in section 11 of the validation report: they are hand-written
  descriptions of the tests, numerals included.
- **Claims stay within the checks.** Each report ends with what it does not show.
- **The monitor recommends; it never acts.** When a threshold trips, it writes a recommendation with its evidence;
  nothing retrains on its own.

## Data

- **Demand:** Hydro-Québec open data, "Historique de la demande d'électricité au Québec", hourly, from 2019.
- **Weather forecast:** NOAA's National Blend of Models NBS guidance for station CYUL (Montréal-Trudeau), from the
  Iowa Environmental Mesonet's archive. Limits: one forecast point stands for the whole province; NOAA's model
  changes over the years are not tracked, so the series is not homogeneous; and no revision of any source is
  modelled, a forecast's arrival time being assumed from its issue time.
- **Observed weather:** Environment and Climate Change Canada hourly station observations from climate.weather.gc.ca,
  for one station in each of six population centres (`config/stations.toml`), for data quality, v1's model and the
  optimistic bound.

Data is fetched by script and never committed. The licence terms of every source, quoted with their URLs, are in
[`docs/data-licences.md`](docs/data-licences.md). Each report also gives the reference to ECCC's site in the form its
FAQ asks for, with the date the data was retrieved.

> Demand data: Hydro-Québec, "Historique de la demande d'électricité au Québec" (https://donnees.hydroquebec.com/explore/dataset/historique-demande-electricite-quebec/), licensed CC BY-NC 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/4.0/). Hydro-Québec offers this data for information only, without warranty of quality; it is not official data. This project checked it, masked or corrected a few hours (each case documented) and aggregated it; it does not redistribute the dataset, and the reports quote only a few hourly values from it, as evidence.
>
> Weather data: Environment and Climate Change Canada, used under the Open Government Licence – Canada (https://open.canada.ca/en/open-government-licence-canada).
>
> Weather forecasts: NOAA National Blend of Models NBS guidance for station CYUL (Montréal-Trudeau), downloaded from the Iowa Environmental Mesonet archive of Iowa State University (https://mesonet.agron.iastate.edu/). This project interpolated these three-hourly forecasts to hourly values and converted them to degrees Celsius: the values it uses are modified and are not original NOAA data.
>
> Neither Hydro-Québec, Environment and Climate Change Canada, NOAA nor the Iowa Environmental Mesonet produced, reviewed or endorsed this work, and the project is affiliated with neither NOAA nor the Iowa Environmental Mesonet.
>
> Built with Claude Code under the repository owner's direction.

No independent human reviewed the code: the reviews were made by AI agents in fresh contexts and by another vendor's
AI model, which is not independent validation in SR 11-7's sense.

## Continuous integration

`.github/workflows/checks.yml` runs the offline tests (every injected break included) and the public-safety scan on
every branch push and on every pull request, a fork's included, checked out at the pull request's own head commit
rather than its merge commit, which the history tests refuse. CI's scan covers paths,
credentials, forbidden files, every file in the history and every commit and tag message, but not private names:
those live in a gitignored list, so only the local `valiwatt safety` checks them.
